title: Belgrade Commands Pale: Milošević Presses Karadžić on Vance-Owen
sources: ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), Belgrade-Pale relationship findings
UN Doc S/25479 (Report of the Co-Chairmen on the Vance-Owen plan, 8 April 1993)
content:
The Bosnian Serb war effort was sustained from Belgrade. Personnel, fuel, ammunition, pay for officers of the Bosnian Serb army, and the diplomatic shelter of the rump Yugoslav state all flowed from Serbia under President Slobodan Milošević. The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) examined this dependence at length. It made the relationship between Belgrade and the Pale leadership the single most consequential lever in the entire Bosnian Serb project — and the one most prone to rupture, because the interests of the patron and the client were not identical.

By the spring of 1993, Milošević had concluded that the Vance-Owen Plan, whatever its defects from a Serb maximalist standpoint, offered a path to lifting the international sanctions that were strangling Serbia’s economy. He therefore pressed Radovan Karadžić to accept it. Karadžić signed the plan in Athens at the end of March under this pressure, then carried it back to the Bosnian Serb assembly at Pale. There the bond between patron and client snapped: on 5–6 May 1993 the assembly defied Belgrade and rejected the plan, submitting it to a referendum that confirmed the rejection.

The episode is one of the clearest demonstrations in the war that patron leverage had limits. Milošević controlled the supply lines, but he did not control the assembly’s vote, and the Bosnian Serb leadership proved willing to absorb Belgrade’s displeasure rather than surrender the territory the plan would have cost them. The rejection deepened Serbia’s sanctions ordeal and began the slow estrangement that would culminate in Belgrade’s formal embargo on the Bosnian Serbs in 1994.

For the Pale leadership the choice was therefore between deference and defiance. To acknowledge Belgrade’s pressure was to preserve the lifeline at the cost of accepting a map the leadership detested. To resist it was to assert an independent war aim at the risk of the patron relationship that armed and fed the entire enterprise. History took the path of defiance; the cost arrived later, in isolation.
